title: Raga Asa
hook: the raga of hope, and the ballad sung while the sky is still dark

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Gauri, and your line was peace in gauri. Did a Gauri shabad find its way into your day, even for a minute? A new week starts now. Day one thousand seventy-two.

Long before sunrise, the street outside a gurdwara is still dark, a dog barks somewhere, and a few cars pull in with their headlights on. Inside, the lights are already up. Someone uncovers a harmonium. A tabla player taps the drumhead, listening for the pitch. People drift in with their heads covered, sit on the carpet, and the singing begins before the birds do. What they're singing has a name: the Asa di Var, the ballad in Asa. Today the Granth turns to a new raga, and this is the one that greets the morning.
screen: `STILL DARK OUTSIDE.` → `THE SINGING STARTS FIRST.` → `THE BALLAD IN ASA.`

segments.voice: Raga Asa is the next great section of the Guru Granth Sahib, coming right after Gauri. In Punjabi, asa is also an everyday word for hope, and Sikh tradition likes to hear that in the raga's name: the raga of hope. Its mood is described as longing that leans forward, a hope that something good is on its way. That fits the hour it's sung. By Sikh custom the Asa di Var belongs to the morning, and in gurdwaras it's sung while the day is still breaking. A var is a ballad, built of stanzas called pauris, with short verses called saloks set between them. In this one, the saloks come from Guru Nanak and Guru Angad. Here's one of Guru Angad's, given in plain English. If a hundred moons rose, and a thousand suns climbed the sky, with all that light there would still be deep darkness without the Guru. Hear that at dawn and it lands differently. The sun is coming up anyway; the salok says outside light isn't the whole story. There's a light the Sikh Gurus point to that a sunrise can't supply, the light of the Guru's word. So the ballad is sung right at the edge of morning, while one kind of light is arriving, to ask for the other. Hope at dawn, then, isn't a mood of forced cheer. It's facing the day before it has shown its hand, and starting it with the Word.
screen: `ASA: THE RAGA OF HOPE.` · `SUNG AS THE DAY BREAKS.` · `A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.` · `STILL DARK WITHOUT THE GURU.` · then, large: `HOPE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet the morning early, at least in your mind. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Picture the sky the way it looks just before sunrise, not dark, not light, that gray-blue in between. Hold that picture. Now let one hope come up, a real one, small or large, for today or for someone you love. Don't polish it. Just let it sit there in the half-light. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once and leave the hope with it. If you don't, keep it company quietly. Tomorrow, if you're up early, play a recording of the Asa di Var while it's still dark. The bell holds the time.
Raga Asa. The raga tradition hears as hope, home of the Asa di Var, the ballad sung while the morning breaks. Today's word.
Your line: hope at dawn. Tomorrow morning, before you check anything, give the first minute to one hope, and to whatever light you lean on. Day one thousand seventy-two.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras the kirtan of the Asa di Var is commonly sung in the early morning, with ragis singing Guru Nanak's pauris and the saloks between them, and the congregation sitting and listening as the day begins.
